content: {"takeaways": ["The registered framing estimate (H1) is positive but imprecise: its interval includes zero.", "The secondary policy-attitude result is a documented deviation: the registered age covariate was not collected as planned.", "The effect was larger among Democrats than Republicans in the registered heterogeneity test.", "Simulated data; nothing here is an empirical finding."], "summary": "In a two-arm online survey experiment with simulated data (N = 387 in the analysis sample), a paragraph describing immigrants' economic contributions was associated with a higher pro-immigration attitude index than a neutral paragraph; the registered H1 estimate is positive but imprecise, with an interval that includes zero. The secondary policy-attitude test (H2) is reported as a deviation because the registered age covariate was not collected as a continuous variable. The registered partisan heterogeneity test (S1) shows a larger effect among Democrats than Republicans. Exploratory analyses suggest the effect is not driven by a single item and is robust to excluding attention-check failures. A silicon sample of LLM personas moves in the same direction with a smaller, imprecise estimate; it is not evidence about human respondents.", "design_notes": "Assignment was recorded by the survey platform in the embedded field `condition`. Completion was the only sample exclusion.", "results": {"H1": "The registered primary estimate is positive but imprecise; its confidence interval includes zero, so the data do not establish an effect.", "H2": "Supported, but tagged as a deviation: age enters as bracket indicators rather than years because age was collected only in brackets. The adjusted estimate should be read with that substitution in mind.", "S1": "The registered interaction is in the expected direction: the per-level estimates show a larger effect among Democrats than Republicans, and the interaction term is statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels. The two-party subsample has 290 respondents."}, "exploratory": {"E1": "All three items move in the pro-immigration direction; the index effect is not an artifact of one item.", "E2": "Dropping attention-check failures leaves the estimate essentially unchanged.", "E3": "Effects decline across the ideology scale; this was not registered and should be treated as hypothesis-generating."}, "silicon": "The silicon estimate has the same sign as the human estimate but is smaller and imprecise with 60 personas; the comparison is descriptive only.", "limitations": "The data are simulated. The sample is an opt-in panel, so effects may not generalize. The age covariate deviation changes the H2 specification. Exploratory and silicon results are not pre-registered and should not be cited as confirmatory evidence. The literature note is minimal and drawn from a small automated search.", "abstract": "In a two-arm online survey experiment with simulated data (N = 387 in the analysis sample), a paragraph describing immigrants' economic contributions was associated with a higher pro-immigration attitude index than a neutral paragraph; the registered H1 estimate is positive but imprecise, with an interval that includes zero. The secondary policy-attitude test (H2) is reported as a deviation because the registered age covariate was not collected as a continuous variable. The registered partisan heterogeneity test (S1) shows a larger effect among Democrats than Republicans. Exploratory analyses suggest the effect is not driven by a single item and is robust to excluding attention-check failures. A silicon sample of LLM personas moves in the same direction with a smaller, imprecise estimate; it is not evidence about human respondents.", "revision_notes": ["K1: The abstract, the first takeaway and the H1 note now say the framing estimate is positive but imprecise instead of claiming a shift.", "G1: The S1 note states the two-party subsample size (290 respondents).", "R1: Same change as G1."]}
